front: What is the shell, and which one does almost every Linux distribution use by default?
back: A program that reads each line you type, works out what you mean, starts the right program and shows its output. Bash (Bourne Again SHell).

front: What are the three jobs the shell does with a command line?
back: It splits the line into words, expands special characters (`$HOME`, `~`, `*`) and runs the first word as the command with the others as input.

front: How do you repeat the last command, command 42, or search old commands?
back: `!!` repeats the last line, `!42` repeats line 42 of `history`, and Ctrl+R searches the history as you type. Bash stores it in `~/.bash_history`.

front: What do Tab, the up arrow and Ctrl+C do in Bash?
back: Tab completes a name, the up arrow brings back the previous line and Ctrl+C stops a running program.

front: What is a builtin, and why must `cd` be one?
back: A builtin is part of Bash itself (`cd`, `echo`, `export`, `type`, `history`). An external program could only change its own directory, never the shell’s.

front: What does `type NAME` tell you?
back: Whether the name is a shell builtin, an external file (it shows the full path), an alias or a keyword. `type -t NAME` prints just `builtin`, `file`, `alias` or `keyword`.

front: `echo` exists as a builtin and as `/usr/bin/echo`. Which one runs?
back: The builtin, because the shell checks builtins first.

front: Which directories hold executables on the exam list, and what do `/bin` and `/sbin` link to on modern Debian?
back: `/bin`, `/usr/bin`, `/sbin` and `/usr/sbin`. On modern Debian `/bin` and `/sbin` are symbolic links to `/usr/bin` and `/usr/sbin`.

front: What do the `s` in `sbin` and the directory `/usr/local/bin` stand for?
back: `sbin` means system administration programs, meant for the administrator. `/usr/local/bin` holds programs the administrator installed by hand.

front: In `ls -l -a /usr/local/bin`, which word is the command, which are options and which is the argument?
back: `ls` is the command, `-l` and `-a` are options and `/usr/local/bin` is the argument.

front: Can short and long options be combined?
back: Short options usually can: `ls -la` equals `ls -l -a`. Long options (`--all`) cannot be combined.

front: What do `echo -n` and `echo -e` do?
back: `-n` leaves out the final newline. `-e` turns backslash sequences like `\t` (tab) and `\n` (new line) into the real characters.

front: What does a semicolon do on a command line?
back: It separates commands that run one after the other: `echo first; echo second`.

front: Why does `echo hello      world` print only one space between the words?
back: The shell splits at every run of spaces, so the extra spaces vanish. Quotes make it one argument and keep them.

front: How do you set a variable in Bash, and how do you read it?
back: `game=Pixel` with no spaces around `=`; read it with a dollar sign: `echo $game`. Names are case sensitive.

front: What is the difference between a local and an environment variable?
back: A local variable is known only to this shell. After `export name` it becomes an environment variable, and programs started from the shell get a copy.

front: Ada runs `RELEASE=0.9` and then starts her build, but the build can’t see it. What is missing?
back: `export RELEASE=0.9` (or `export RELEASE`). Without it the variable stays local to the shell.

front: Can a child program change a variable in the shell that started it?
back: No. A copy goes down to child programs; changes never travel back up.

front: What is the difference between `env` and `set`?
back: `env` prints the environment variables only. `set` prints everything the shell knows, including local variables and functions, so it is much longer.

front: What do `HOME`, `USER`, `SHELL` and `PATH` hold?
back: `HOME`: your home directory. `USER`: your user name. `SHELL`: your login shell. `PATH`: the directories searched for commands.

front: How does the shell use `PATH`?
back: It looks in each listed directory, separated by colons and in order, and runs the first match. If none has it, you get `command not found`.

front: Why does `run.sh` in the current directory give "command not found" while `./run.sh` works?
back: The current directory `.` is deliberately not in `PATH`. `./run.sh` gives a path, so no search is needed.

front: Jonas put a tool in `/home/jonas/bin` and gets `command not found`. How does he add the directory to `PATH` for this session?
back: `PATH="$PATH:/home/jonas/bin"`, which keeps the old value. To make it last, put it in a start-up file like `~/.bashrc`.

front: How do you remove a variable?
back: `unset name`, without a dollar sign.

front: What are the three quoting tools in Bash?
back: A backslash escapes the one next character. Single quotes make everything inside literal. Double quotes are literal except that `$` (variables) and a few others still work.

front: With `name=Mira`, what do `echo "$name"`, `echo '$name'` and `echo \$name` print?
back: `Mira`, `$name` and `$name`. Only double quotes (and no quotes) expand the variable.

front: A sprite is called `slime attack.png`. Why does `rm slime attack.png` go wrong?
back: The space splits it into two arguments, so `rm` tries to delete two files. `rm "slime attack.png"` deletes one.

front: What is command substitution, and does it work in single quotes?
back: `$(command)` is replaced by what the command prints. It works in double quotes but not in single quotes.

front: Why does `echo "*"` print a star while `echo *` lists file names?
back: Quotes switch off the special meaning, so the shell does not expand the `*`. Unquoted, the shell replaces it with matching names.

front: What is the order in which Bash looks up the first word of a command line?
back: Alias, keyword, function, builtin, then the programs in the `PATH` directories. `type -t NAME` shows which one wins.

front: What does `!word` do at the prompt, and what does `history -c` do?
back: `!word` repeats the most recent line that starts with `word`. `history -c` clears the shell's history list.

front: How do you read the prompt `mira@tuxpixel:~$`?
back: User `mira`, host `tuxpixel`, current directory `~` (the home directory); `$` marks a normal user, `#` marks root.
